Mike:   It’s all about empathy. They need to understand what it’s like to live in Norwich or Costessey where the cost of living keeps going up. Not everyone lives in London or the South where things might be more manageable.   Arthur:   That's the thing. They just don’t get it. Our eastern England wages, they were never particularly high. We worked hard locally but never ended up with city salaries. The small pensions we were expecting are now being reduced further and further.   Sarah:   I often think about the younger generation. We've got a lot to cover today, haven't we? I've been thinking about how to help you with marketing for Honest Skincare. You know I've spent years teaching business English to entrepreneurs around the world, and I've seen a fair few do's and don'ts when it comes to online marketing.      Thanks, actually, that's really helpful. I feel like I'm just winging it so far with my marketing strategy. I get how important it is, but I just don't know where to start. Like how do I stand out online when there are so many established brands out there?      One of the key places to start is by identifying your unique selling proposition, or USP. What makes your skincare products different from others? For example, are your products completely natural, or do you also cater to specific skin types?      Ah, that’s a good question. Honest Skincare is all about using clean, natural ingredients. No harsh chemicals and nothing tested on animals.      Great! That’s a strong starting point. You can use that as your main differentiator. For example, “Clean skincare for clear skin, without the nasty stuff.”      I like that. So how do I actually get that across in my online presence? I mean, we’re talking about a website, social media, and possibly even email marketing.      Well, let’s start with the website. You need a clean, simple design that instantly conveys who you are and what you stand for. Avoid clutter, focus on those natural ingredients, and let’s not forget to keep it user-friendly.      Makes sense. That and maybe some testimonials from customers to build credibility.      Absolutely, testimonials are key for building trust. But for social media, it's just as important to keep it consistent so potential customers know what they're getting into. Think of it like your brand's personality.      Personality? Like, we're not just posting about the products but also about the process, right? I started this business because I got frustrated with the beauty industry's greenwashing and stuff.      Exactly! You could share behind-the-scenes content, like how you source your natural ingredients or any community projects you might be involved in. It helps if you can show the human side of your business.      I see. So we need a mix of product info and behind-the-scenes content to build a community around our brand?

Speaker_1    Oh, hi love. Want a cup of tea while we talk? That would be lovely, thank you.      So, have you seen the news today? News? There's keeps coming in every day, isn't there? Yes, but today was particularly disturbing. This new policy about welfare for the long-term unemployed. It's really made me think about our own situation.      Which situation? The recent cuts to the support we get. I suppose you know all about it.      I do, but aren't you retired? You didn't work very long in the public sector, right? Past tense – I'm retired now, yes. So, I'm not affected that way. But this is about all the changes to benefits for those who are still trying to find work or are long-term unemployed. The news today was rather disheartening. They seem to be making it even tougher for people to survive.      I see. It's quite challenging, isn't it? I feel for all those affected. But isn't it also a bit about trying to encourage people to find work through less generous benefits? That’s the policy argument, yes… but in practice it doesn't always lead to people finding jobs immediately. The issue is the lack of opportunities, and sometimes the lack of support to help people get back into work. I just worry about our friends back home who are in similar situations. The idea of a safety net is quite important.      True, but as a teacher, I've seen and heard a lot of arguments from both sides. This generation differs in so many ways from when we were younger. Definitely. I remember when I was in teaching, there was always an emphasis on education being the key to better opportunities. And it's still true, but now there are just so many other obstacles.      Did you have any students who ended up in this situation? Yes, quite a few. I recall particularly one young man who had all the potential but just couldn't seem to get a stable job. The issue was often more about the wider economic situation and job market than his abilities or drive.      I've seen the same thing. But interestingly, some schools are starting to offer more vocational training alongside traditional subjects. Seems like a step forward, trying to link education to viable job markets. Yes, that's a good idea.

Maybe we could even arrange a film night sometime? I have a subscription that...      That sounds like a great idea!

Oh, I don't know, Mum. I'm so worried about the upcoming GCSE exams. The kids at school are really struggling with their English literature.      Oh, darling, now, don't you worry too much – you're doing a fantastic job as their teacher!      Thank you, but it's not just about me – it's about the kids. This past year has been so tough on everyone. The changes in the curriculum keeps coming, and alongside it, the pressure to perform...      True, but think about how much they've grown, despite everything. And you're guiding them through all that. You're doing more than teaching - you're mentoring, supporting, and inspiring them.      That's kind of you to say, but sometimes I feel like I'm not doing enough. You know, your generation seems to have managed with barely any help at home, and we barely scrape by with all these support tools for the kids.      We scraped by on our own merits, no support groups, no tutors...but the pressure was different. We had different expectations, I think. But it proves the point - the kids are adapting, and so are you. Adapting to new challenges means you're growing, Helen. That's important. Now, let’s not worry about that for a moment. I know how much you loved that when you were my age too. And it's eco-friendly, if I remember correctly?      Yes, it's electric. It feels so modern and quite economical in the long run compared to petrol or diesel.      That’s good. We need more of that. Especially with the fuel prices nowadays, it will save you a lot. I know that was never much of an issue while I was...ushering for the courts. Fuel prices can’t be the most pressing concern when you're dealing with...legal disagreements all day.

I've been thinking a lot about our idea for an online platform for collaborative learning these past few days. It could really disrupt the way young people learn, wouldn't it? Absolutely! I was thinking about those ASMR videos people almost unintentionally learn from.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we went hot air ballooning over Bristol? You told me that story countless times! But I love hearing it every time! Alright, alright! “Nevil, dear, what's all this about Manchester then? You haven't talked about it for ages."      "Ah, yes, Manchester. It was where my Uncle Arthur moved about a quarter-century ago, after that socialism nonsense of his got him right chucked out of Tamworth."      “Socialism? Arthur keeps coming backwards and forwards on that. Reminds me of my mate Jimmy, used to argue politics 'til the cows came home."      "Exactly, even his politics was as wishy-washy as a Norfolk village in the rain. Anyway, Manchester. It's not somewhere I have any sentimental attachment to, but Arthur hated it, I recall."      “He hated it? But why? You'd think him and his socialism would adore the throngs and the council or whatever, he was firmly For the People and All That."      “That's Arthur. He assumed, while the rest of us were seeing the benefits of deregulation and Thatcher's brave new world, the reality was quite different. He wanted people to manage their lives, for community, for working together for the common good. Which sounds lovely, but Manchester's got its... its rough edges, as I heard from him."      “Like what rough edges? doesn't sound ideal for an old chap like himself.”      “Well, if I recall right, he was really taken aback by the poverty, the sheer number of rough sleepers, and the stark difference in living conditions. We talked a lot about it when I visited couple of years ago before Alzheimer's got the better of his ins and outs. It hit him hard, I think. You know how it is with some folks; they can plan and argue, but reality sometimes presses hard against what you're sure should be."      “That's a right real world lesson, innit? We have our beliefs and our theories about how things should go, but once you face the bricks and mortar of real life, all those fancy words and pictures we paint in our heads... they just don't match up.”      “Exactly. You could say the same for his politics or this sandwich. I've eyed the recipe for fifteen years, promised to make it just so, but when I finally do, it never quite is. Still, it's enough, isn't it? They still eat it, and mostly enjoy.”      “Enough. Yes. Sometimes successful change is less about making grand statements or overhauling the whole system and more about a small sandwiched lunch that's just right, even if it ain’t perfect."

Oh, I bumped into an entire family from Bexley when I was in Italy last year! It was such a bizarre moment, finding familiar accents in the most unexpected places. Made me feel right at home. He was such a sweet boy. Always loved animals.      He still does. The local pet adoption agency has been doing charity events, and I’ve been thinking of taking him there for a visit.

Hey Mum, did you hear about that equality vote last year?      Oi, yeah, didn’t it change everything? Well, at least talked about a lot. What are you on about, again? You got a voice like a rusty gate now, all this interest in politics.      Oh haha, isn’t that one of your usual complaints? Like how you get "vital" with that socialism chat of yours every time your favorite show gets cancelled. I’m just genuinely curious about how it affected us. I mean, how is it going to make people treat each other better?      Well, to be fair, there have been many changes in the last few years. I’ve been following it from a London viewpoint. It’s like the whole of England talking about it - in every pub, in every news broadcast, even discussed at school.      That’s what I mean. Weirdly, I didn’t hear much about it here in Cork, even though we’re in Ireland. But when we visited you in London last holiday, it was all anyone talked about.      So, you were there in the thick of it this time last year and nothing registers until it affects you directly? Oh, I’ve voted with the most colourful of paintbrushes while the rest of the world has been in politics.      It’s not like that. I just... well, we talk about Irish stuff at school, but the UK is... A bit distant. Speaking of distant, how is the new baby doing?      Oh, the baby. Doing wonderfully, thank you for asking. Though doesn’t sleep much, loves to wake me up with the enthusiasm that rivals my early morning political sessions. Except, he’s on the side of "Argh, let the mommy sleep!"      Hahaha! He’s growing up to be a good little socialist then?      Oh God, please no! I want him to be peaceful and maybe, just maybe, interested in sport - something to compensate for my lack of interest.      Don’t worry, he’s got time. Let’s say, by his 18th birthday, if he still hasn’t found his calling, we can discuss it over a pint in a pub in London.      Over a pint of Guinness, you mean? Maybe. Though I swear, if I ever hear another argument about Marxist theory while he’s still in nappies, I’m out.      You just worry about not introducing him to your embarrassing book club readings.

Like with essays, we're used to questioning facts and sources. Is that why we like structured arguments even in art discussions?      Exactly, because we can't "prove" an artist's intentions or the validity of their emotions like we can with facts. But I think that's where the fun is. It also links to how we respond to games, right? Video games can't be proven 'better' or 'worse' by objective measures.      I get this argument a lot about game design. 'This game is better' usually means it's more fun or accessible for certain people. And while the 'fun' part can be somewhat quantifiable, like player engagement and time spent, the core subjective experience? That's where art comes in, isn't it?      Yeah, it feels like art breaks the mold in suggesting that subjective experience is okay to be discussed, even without 'right' or 'wrong' answers. Whereas in essays, we're trained to argue for a point, to defend a view.      That’s really interesting because it makes me think about how we approach our own future, our old age, even just our university work. Do we base our choices on what feels right, or do we think in terms of what's 'best' or 'safest' and try to measure that?      Oh, we do that all the time. Like, is this course the best for our career or should I switch to something I enjoy more but might be less 'useful'?      But when you think about it, if almost all of us are just following paths that feel right or are expected of us, and we're not really questioning deeply what we want in the long run... does that make us more or less like characters in a well-designed game?      Wow, that's... a game-design perspective on life choices! But no, I mean, if we think of our life as a game where we're always trying to level up or gain skills, then maybe it's a mix.

We've got enough food today to feed a small village, if we could only figure out how to cook it all.      No, the mountain of leftovers is entirely your doing, sister. Isn't that a sign of how much she trusts you?
